name: Frontend Interview Practice
summary: Seven anonymous frontend challenges with guided steps, three React/TypeScript solutions each, and matching Python logic examples.

questions.title: Dynamic Rectangular Board
questions.summary: Render independently sized rows and columns and explain React identity, state, refs, and memoization.
questions.prompt: Build a React board with independently configurable rows and columns. Render zero-based coordinates in each cell and keep the layout readable. This exercise focuses on rendering, not game rules.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.explanation: Six cells cover the Cartesian product of the two row indexes and three column indexes.

constraints: Practice UI dimensions are integers from 1 to 50; the model also accepts zero for empty-grid tests.
Do not assume rows equal columns.
Explain useRef, useMemo, and useCallback without adding them solely to sound advanced.

evaluation.intent: Render independently sized rows and columns and explain React identity, state, refs, and memoization. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Render a non-square case before adding abstractions.
Explain that keys preserve sibling identity and do not prevent rerenders.
Keep correctness independent of memoization.

acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Build a React board with independently configurable rows and columns. Render zero-based coordinates in each cell and keep the layout readable. This exercise focuses on rendering, not game rules.

solutionTracks.title: Nested rows
solutionTracks.summary: Build the rectangular structure explicitly, then render one row at a time.

steps.title: Clarify the rectangle
steps.explanation: Ask whether rows and columns vary independently and whether cells hold state. This baseline renders coordinates only.

steps.title: Make the model
steps.explanation: Allocate a new inner array for each row. Append one cell per column so rectangular cases work.

steps.title: Render a small example
steps.explanation: Render 2 rows and 3 columns first. Check the final coordinate is 1,2 and all six cells appear.

steps.title: Explain identity and hooks
steps.explanation: Coordinate keys suit a stateless positional grid. Reordering entity data requires entity IDs. A ref does not trigger rendering; memo hooks are optional performance tools.

solutionTracks.explanation: Every coordinate is produced exactly once by the row/column product. Each inner array is separate, so editing one row cannot accidentally edit another. The three approaches differ in representation and composition, while all render the same number of cells.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: Avoid Array(rows).fill(sharedRow) and Python [shared_row] * rows: both alias the same row object.
All approaches render every cell. A generator does not reduce the final DOM size, and memoization is not required for correctness.

complexity.space: O(rows × columns + rows)

python.explanation: Run this equivalent data model and behavior locally with Python 3.11 or later, without a browser. The TypeScript interface handles React hooks, DOM events, focus, and rendering.

questions.title: Randomized Zero Matrix
questions.summary: Select exactly k distinct zero positions while keeping generated React state stable and testable.
questions.prompt: Create a 10×10 matrix filled with ones except for exactly k randomly chosen distinct positions containing zeros. Store the result in React state and regenerate on an explicit button press.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.explanation: Exactly two distinct positions are zero; the specific positions depend on the random draws.

constraints: k = 10 is an authored practice default, not a requirement stated in the brief.
Use k between 0 and 100.
Unrelated renders must preserve the current generated board.

evaluation.intent: Select exactly k distinct zero positions while keeping generated React state stable and testable. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Distinguish exact count from Bernoulli per-cell probability.
Account for both sampling work and the materialized output.
Inject deterministic randomness for tests instead of asserting a particular unseeded board.

solutionTracks.title: Full Fisher–Yates shuffle
solutionTracks.summary: Select exactly k unique cells before projecting indexes into independent matrix rows.

steps.title: Set the sampling contract
steps.explanation: Clarify exact count versus independent per-cell probability. Our practice contract uses exact k, from zero to the number of cells.

steps.title: Select unique indexes
steps.explanation: Shuffle the full index pool in place, working backward, then take the first k. This is the simplest baseline to explain.

steps.title: Build fresh rows
steps.explanation: Turn selected flat indexes into zeros and all other cells into ones. Allocate each row independently.

steps.title: Keep random work stable
steps.explanation: Store generated output in state. Regenerate only after an explicit action; use an injected random function for repeatable tests.

solutionTracks.explanation: At each step, Fisher–Yates swaps a uniformly chosen remaining item into the current position. The first k positions of the resulting permutation form a sample without replacement. Distinct indexes guarantee distinct zero cells.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: The uniformity argument assumes independent uniform random draws in [0, 1). The small seeded generator is a reproducible teaching aid, not cryptographic randomness.
Avoid random sort comparators and unbounded retry-until-unique loops. Count zeros and test k = 0 and k = n.

complexity.space: O(n + rows) output; O(n) selection memory

solutionTracks.title: Partial Fisher–Yates shuffle
solutionTracks.summary: Select exactly k unique cells before projecting indexes into independent matrix rows.

steps.title: Set the sampling contract
steps.explanation: Clarify exact count versus independent per-cell probability. Our practice contract uses exact k, from zero to the number of cells.

steps.title: Select unique indexes
steps.explanation: Swap a random item from the remaining suffix into each of the first k positions. Do not shuffle positions already fixed.

steps.title: Build fresh rows
steps.explanation: Turn selected flat indexes into zeros and all other cells into ones. Allocate each row independently.

steps.title: Keep random work stable
steps.explanation: Store generated output in state. Regenerate only after an explicit action; use an injected random function for repeatable tests.

solutionTracks.explanation: Each iteration chooses uniformly from the remaining suffix and fixes one new selected position. No index can appear twice. Only k swaps are needed, although allocating the pool and rendering the matrix still require O(n) work.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.

Avoid random sort comparators and unbounded retry-until-unique loops. Count zeros and test k = 0 and k = n.

solutionTracks.title: Reservoir sampling
solutionTracks.summary: Select exactly k unique cells before projecting indexes into independent matrix rows.

steps.title: Set the sampling contract
steps.explanation: Clarify exact count versus independent per-cell probability. Our practice contract uses exact k, from zero to the number of cells.

steps.title: Select unique indexes
steps.explanation: Keep k indexes while visiting the remaining population. Replace only when a random index falls inside the reservoir.

steps.title: Build fresh rows
steps.explanation: Turn selected flat indexes into zeros and all other cells into ones. Allocate each row independently.

steps.title: Keep random work stable
steps.explanation: Store generated output in state. Regenerate only after an explicit action; use an injected random function for repeatable tests.

solutionTracks.explanation: The reservoir starts with k indexes. At stream position i, an index enters with probability k/(i+1), replacing a uniformly chosen reservoir slot. Induction gives every processed index the same inclusion probability. It saves selection memory, but the materialized matrix still costs O(n).
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: The uniformity argument assumes independent uniform random draws in [0, 1). The small seeded generator is a reproducible teaching aid, not cryptographic randomness.
Avoid random sort comparators and unbounded retry-until-unique loops. Count zeros and test k = 0 and k = n.

complexity.space: O(n + rows) output; O(k) selection memory

questions.title: Click-to-place 5×5 Game
questions.summary: Model legal turns and detect contiguous horizontal or vertical wins without adding unstated game rules.
questions.prompt: Build a 5×5 board where clicking an empty cell places a token in that exact cell. Alternate R and Y after valid nonterminal moves. Four contiguous horizontal or vertical tokens win; stop the game and display the result.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.output: R wins; later clicks leave the state unchanged.
examples.explanation: The new token completes four adjacent tokens on the allowed horizontal axis.

constraints: R starts as an authored practice default.
Ignore invalid moves without changing the player.
Stop after a win; handle a full board as a draw.
Diagonal wins are deliberately excluded.

evaluation.intent: Model legal turns and detect contiguous horizontal or vertical wins without adding unstated game rules. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Implement a visible board before optimizing winner detection.
Keep invalid moves and terminal moves from corrupting turn state.
Demonstrate a gap and a diagonal as counterexamples to overbroad win detection.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Working behavior
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Build a 5×5 board where clicking an empty cell places a token in that exact cell. Alternate R and Y after valid nonterminal moves. Four contiguous horizontal or vertical tokens win; stop the game and display the result.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Evidence and communication
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Walk through the example, show an edge case, and connect each state change to an observable result.

redFlags.title: Changes the contract silently
redFlags.explanation: Adding familiar rules or dropping explicit requirements can produce working code that solves a different problem.

redFlags.title: Claims an optimization without accounting for costs
redFlags.explanation: Separate model computation, immutable copying, network latency, and rendering before comparing approaches.

solutionTracks.title: Full-board scan
solutionTracks.summary: Keep each move atomic: validate, place, detect terminal state, and change turns only after a valid nonterminal move.

steps.title: Render before optimizing
steps.explanation: Build the requested rectangle and show R and Y tokens. State explicitly whether clicking chooses a cell or a column.

steps.title: Make one atomic transition
steps.explanation: Use one game-state object. A pure move function returns the old state for occupied cells, full columns, out-of-range coordinates, or a finished game.

steps.title: Check the actual rule
steps.explanation: Every possible horizontal and vertical start is checked, and only four contiguous matching tokens qualify. Scanning all possible windows is easy to verify and adequate for this tiny board.

steps.title: Prove the boundary cases
steps.explanation: Test a fourth token at each edge, a gap that must not win, a diagonal that must not win, and clicks after the game ends. Track successful moves for draw detection.

steps.title: Explain the cost
steps.explanation: Separate winner detection from immutable array copying and rendering. Keep the simplest version unless the interviewer asks for refinement.

solutionTracks.explanation: Every possible horizontal and vertical start is checked, and only four contiguous matching tokens qualify. Scanning all possible windows is easy to verify and adequate for this tiny board. The state transition updates the board, result, move count, and player together, so an invalid move cannot consume a turn. A full board without a winner is a draw.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: Diagonal wins are an extension, not part of this brief. Never substitute familiar game rules without asking.
For fixed 5×5 or 6×7 sizes the work is bounded. Generalized bounds below distinguish detection from total move cost.
Read board state from the functional updater to avoid stale event-handler snapshots.

complexity.space: O(RC) board; O(R+C) transient row-copy allocation

solutionTracks.summary: Keep each move atomic: validate, place, detect terminal state, and change turns only after a valid nonterminal move.

questions.title: Recursive File Explorer
questions.summary: Combine both supplied tree briefs into a recursive explorer with explicit expansion-state behavior.
questions.prompt: Render nested file/folder mock data using FileExplorer and a recursive FileItem. Support expanding and collapsing folders, an empty-data message, indentation, and vertical hierarchy lines for expanded children.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.input: src folder contains components folder containing FileExplorer.tsx.
examples.output: Opening src reveals components; opening components reveals the file one level deeper.
examples.explanation: Closing src hides every descendant. On reopening, descendant expansion follows the selected approach’s documented ownership policy.

constraints: Use globally unique stable IDs, not filenames, as keys.
Retain recursive FileItem rendering in all three approaches.
Specify whether child expansion resets or persists when an ancestor closes.
Data is a finite acyclic tree; cycle validation is a follow-up for untrusted input.

evaluation.intent: Combine both supplied tree briefs into a recursive explorer with explicit expansion-state behavior. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Use the explicit node type to handle empty folders.
Explain local unmount/reset behavior versus controlled expansion.
Match indentation and hierarchy lines to nested structure.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Working behavior
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Render nested file/folder mock data using FileExplorer and a recursive FileItem. Support expanding and collapsing folders, an empty-data message, indentation, and vertical hierarchy lines for expanded children.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Evidence and communication
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Walk through the example, show an edge case, and connect each state change to an observable result.

redFlags.title: Changes the contract silently
redFlags.explanation: Adding familiar rules or dropping explicit requirements can produce working code that solves a different problem.

redFlags.title: Claims an optimization without accounting for costs
redFlags.explanation: Separate model computation, immutable copying, network latency, and rendering before comparing approaches.

solutionTracks.title: Recursive local state
solutionTracks.summary: Let each folder component own its expanded flag for the shortest implementation.

steps.title: State the tree contract
steps.explanation: Use finite acyclic mock data, globally unique IDs, and a file/folder discriminated type. A folder may have no children.

steps.title: Render one node recursively
steps.explanation: FileItem displays a file name or a folder button. Render child FileItems only when the folder is open.

steps.title: Choose expansion ownership
steps.explanation: Use one boolean per mounted folder. Closing an ancestor removes its children; their local state resets on reopening.

steps.title: Check empty and nested cases
steps.explanation: Render a no-data message for an empty root list and an empty-folder message for a folder without children. Use nested lists and left borders for hierarchy.

steps.title: Explain limits
steps.explanation: Recursive depth consumes stack space. For untrusted or extremely deep trees, validate cycles and consider a different traversal strategy; that is a follow-up, not this mock-data contract.

solutionTracks.explanation: A recursive renderer matches the tree definition: display the current node, then apply the same rule to each visible child. Stable IDs distinguish equal filenames. Rendering only expanded descendants prevents collapsed content from appearing, while nested lists encode the hierarchy.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: Local expansion resets after ancestor unmounting; controlled and normalized versions preserve it. Both policies are valid when stated explicitly.
Do not use names as keys, mutate a Set in place, or infer a folder from nonempty children. Empty folders still have type folder.
The simple recursive visible-row helper may copy descendant results at each level: O(v × h) worst case. Normalized traversal appends into one accumulator.

complexity.time: UI O(v) traversal; companion O(v × h) worst case; v visible nodes, h depth, e expanded IDs
complexity.space: O(n + e + v + h) including data, expansion, rows, and stack

questions.title: Multi-select with Removable Chips
questions.summary: Model selection and derived filtering while preserving disabled options, keyboard access, and dismissal behavior.
questions.prompt: Build a filterable multi-select. Selecting an enabled option adds a removable chip, clears the input, and removes that option from the dropdown. Show matching disabled options as unavailable. Close outside the component and show No results when nothing matches.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.input: Type "script", choose TypeScript, then remove its chip.
examples.output: TypeScript becomes selected, input clears, and it disappears from results; removal restores it.
examples.explanation: The dropdown is derived from current selection and query, so the two views cannot drift.

constraints: Match anywhere in the label, case-insensitively.
Use explicit IDs; selected options cannot be duplicated.
Disabled options must be visible when matching and rejected by the model.
Support Tab/Enter/Space, Escape, outside pointer dismissal, and visible focus.

evaluation.intent: Model selection and derived filtering while preserving disabled options, keyboard access, and dismissal behavior. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Derive the filtered list rather than storing redundant results.
Reject disabled options even if selection is called programmatically.
Explain focus movement and remove global listeners during cleanup.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Working behavior
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Build a filterable multi-select. Selecting an enabled option adds a removable chip, clears the input, and removes that option from the dropdown. Show matching disabled options as unavailable. Close outside the component and show No results when nothing matches.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Evidence and communication
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Walk through the example, show an edge case, and connect each state change to an observable result.

redFlags.title: Changes the contract silently
redFlags.explanation: Adding familiar rules or dropping explicit requirements can produce working code that solves a different problem.

redFlags.title: Claims an optimization without accounting for costs
redFlags.explanation: Separate model computation, immutable copying, network latency, and rendering before comparing approaches.

solutionTracks.title: Local state and derived options
solutionTracks.summary: Keep selection, query, and open state together; derive visible options on every render.

steps.title: Specify selection identity
steps.explanation: Assign stable option IDs. Selected IDs and query are state; the filtered dropdown is derived, not separately synchronized state.

steps.title: Enforce rules in the model
steps.explanation: Case-insensitive substring matching excludes selected IDs. Disabled options remain visible when matching, but selection is rejected in the transition itself.

steps.title: Compose chips and input
steps.explanation: Place removable buttons and the input inside one visual field. Selecting clears the query; removal makes an option available again.

steps.title: Handle focus and dismissal
steps.explanation: Native buttons provide Tab/Enter/Space operation. Close on outside pointer events, focus leaving the component, and Escape. Clean up the document listener.

steps.title: Explain the chosen organization
steps.explanation: Local state is the baseline. A reducer clarifies growing event rules. A controlled hook helps reuse the model. All three have the same filtering complexity.

solutionTracks.explanation: The visible list is a pure function of options, selected IDs, and query, so removing or selecting cannot leave a stale dropdown. Selection checks run inside the model as well as in disabled buttons. A single transition clears the query and adds the chip atomically.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: Do not present these organization alternatives as three faster filtering algorithms: each scans the option labels.
Native labeled inputs and buttons are intentional here. A full ARIA combobox would also require its complete arrow-key and active-descendant behavior.
Use IDs rather than labels for identity. The supplied labels are unique, but that need not hold for future data.

complexity.time: O(n × L + s) filtering; O(n + s) selection, n options, L label length, s selected IDs
complexity.space: O(n + s) derived options and selection

questions.title: Asynchronous User Repository Matrix
questions.summary: Fetch user counts, handle partial failures, and place results in stable unique cells despite out-of-order requests.
questions.prompt: Fetch up to three users from /userList, retrieve each user’s public owned repository count, and display the users in distinct random positions of a 3×3 grid. Keep positions stable while results arrive and report errors per user.
questions.sourceNote: Original practice adaptation of privately supplied frontend interview briefs. Employer identity and private source documents are omitted. Assumptions and extensions are labeled in the companion lesson.

examples.input: Ada succeeds with 103 repositories; Grace fails; Linus succeeds with 2.
examples.output: Three unique cells retain their assigned users; Grace shows an error while Ada and Linus show their counts.
examples.explanation: Failures and completion order do not change identity or placement.

constraints: Use mocked asynchronous data in the playground.
The corrected GitHub endpoint is /users/{username}/repos?type=owner; follow every page.
Deduplicate usernames case-insensitively as an authored practice rule.
A reload starts a new assignment; unrelated renders and individual responses do not.

evaluation.intent: Fetch user counts, handle partial failures, and place results in stable unique cells despite out-of-order requests. Explain the requirements, build a small working interface, then validate its data model and discuss tradeoffs.
expectedSignals: Notice the source URL typo and pagination limit.
Separate fetching, placement, and rendering.
Prove stale-response suppression with a mock that ignores cancellation.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Working behavior
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Fetch up to three users from /userList, retrieve each user’s public owned repository count, and display the users in distinct random positions of a 3×3 grid. Keep positions stable while results arrive and report errors per user.

acceptanceCriteria.title: Evidence and communication
acceptanceCriteria.explanation: Walk through the example, show an edge case, and connect each state change to an observable result.

redFlags.title: Changes the contract silently
redFlags.explanation: Adding familiar rules or dropping explicit requirements can produce working code that solves a different problem.

redFlags.title: Claims an optimization without accounting for costs
redFlags.explanation: Separate model computation, immutable copying, network latency, and rendering before comparing approaches.

solutionTracks.title: Sequential requests
solutionTracks.summary: Start with the easiest request order to explain and debug, accepting additive latency.

steps.title: Clarify what count means
steps.explanation: Count public owned repositories. Correct the URL to /users/{username}/repos and page through the complete response; private repositories require a different authorization contract.

steps.title: Assign cells before requests
steps.explanation: Fetch up to three usernames, deduplicate case-insensitively, and sample unique positions from nine cells. Store assignments before repository results arrive.

steps.title: Choose request orchestration
steps.explanation: Fetch each user in sequence; capture a failure and continue so one error does not hide other users.

steps.title: Protect lifecycle updates
steps.explanation: Pass cancellation to the adapter and check it again after awaits. On reload or unmount, cancel the old generation so even an adapter that ignores abort cannot publish stale results.

steps.title: Demonstrate adverse outcomes
steps.explanation: Use mock pages with more than 100 repositories, a rate-limit error, and late responses. Show stable positions and successful users alongside failures.

solutionTracks.explanation: Sampling cells without replacement prevents collisions. Binding each request to its preassigned user/index prevents completion order from moving users. Pagination counts every returned page; cancellation checks guard publication even if a transport ignores cancellation. Per-user errors remain data rather than wiping out unrelated successes.
solutionTracks.acceptanceRationale: This implementation meets the practice requirements. Demonstrate edge cases and explain tradeoffs in the interview; meeting this rubric does not guarantee an interview outcome.
tradeoffs: The playground uses deterministic mocks and never calls GitHub. The adapter can use fetch in a local experiment; never embed tokens in browser code.
A paginated listing is not a transactional snapshot. Concurrent repository creation/deletion can affect a live count; tests use fixed pages.
Bounded concurrency is an extension for quota pressure. With at most three users, the parallel baseline is usually sufficient.
Cancellation prevents stale local publication; it does not prove remote work stopped.

complexity.time: O(u + total returned repositories) parsing; requests equal all pages. Latency is the sum of user page chains.
complexity.space: O(u + 100) retained data per active page chain; nine rendered cells

python.explanation: Run this equivalent data model and behavior locally with Python 3.11 or later, without a browser. The TypeScript interface handles React hooks, DOM events, focus, and rendering.

tradeoffs: The playground uses deterministic mocks and never calls GitHub. The adapter can use fetch in a local experiment; never embed tokens in browser code.
A paginated listing is not a transactional snapshot. Concurrent repository creation/deletion can affect a live count; tests use fixed pages.
Bounded concurrency is an extension for quota pressure. With at most three users, the parallel baseline is usually sufficient.
Cancellation prevents stale local publication; it does not prove remote work stopped.

complexity.time: O(u + total returned repositories) parsing; requests equal all pages. Two user chains at a time; progressive completion.
complexity.space: O(u + 100) retained data per active page chain; nine rendered cells

python.explanation: Run this equivalent data model and behavior locally with Python 3.11 or later, without a browser. The TypeScript interface handles React hooks, DOM events, focus, and rendering.
